title: Instruction - Requires the Visual Evidence
questionText: Rate the Requires the Visual Evidence of the Instruction dimension.
questionDescription:
Does solving the task genuinely require the bundled assets — i.e., the instruction points to the image(s) and the defect can't be diagnosed/localized from the text alone?
Assess according to the instructions.md and attached image assets

**NOTE:** Do not use the sandbox to assess. Download the 4 directories, inspect, run Docker, patch, and test code locally.

**NOTE:** If there are multiple bundled assets, this dimension is considered passing if at least one of them is required to fully solve the task.

**NOTE**: Do not use the included trajectories as definitive proof or the sole reason as to whether included assets would be required to fully solve the task. (I.e., just because a model was able to accomplish the task without referencing the image in its trajectory does not automatically mean that the image is completely unnecessary in the context of this project.)

**NOTE**: if included, ignore any alt text for the image.

This should be a judgment call—put yourself in the perspective of the developer. Do the included assets meaningfully assist in diagnosing, pinpointing, or solving the issue? (In a way that's more substantial than simple visualization of the issue.)
It is solvable if it can be done Correctly, Confidently, and Completely; without the image.

Example:
- Instruction.md: "There's a game log bug in which 'a' is used incorrectly when preceding vowel-starting words. Check `bug_example.png` for reference."
- At first glance, this instruction may seem fully solvable without referring to the image—it describes a trivial bug, along with where the bug is encountered.
- However, the image—`bug_example.png`—may paint a different picture by showing the following sentence: "The player was hit by a an Orc for 10 damage!"
- This bug is different from the typical "a-instead-of-an" grammar slip-up—the problem is an extra "a" rather than the wrong usage. Therefore, the image does provide sufficiently helpful context in diagnosing the issue—the specifics of this issue wouldn't have been clear from the instructions, alone.
errorCategories: [All] [All] [Fail - Assests Not Needed]; [All] [All] [Non-Fail Assets misdirected]; [All] [All] [Non-fail - Assets subjectively needed]
answerOptionText:
[Fail – Assets Not Needed]
• The task is fully solvable from the instruction text
• The asset(s) do not add any useful information that is not already present in the instruction text
• The instruction never references the asset(s) so the agent isn't even directed to them

[Non-Fail - Assets misdirected]
The instructions note there is an asset included, but gives no pathing, or incorrect pathing

[Non-fail - Assets subjectively needed]
The task is subjectively solvable from the instruction text alone, but the included visual assets provides helpful context or guidance (beyond simple visualization of the bug)
The instruction points the agent to the asset(s) and the defect can only be diagnosed/localized by viewing them

title: Instruction – Symptom Specificity
questionText: Check the instruction.md file's contents to see if the symptoms are properly listed.
questionDescription:
Instruction check: Verify that the instruction names the affected element by its type, i.e., the thing that looks wrong ("the shadow", "the header labels", "the edges into subgraphs", "the converted chart"), without hinting at the fix. The visible defect and the expected result may be stated in the text or shown through a comparison image the text points to (current vs. reference, before vs. after, original vs. converted, "like the correct ones next to them"). Which specific instance has the problem (which object, which row) may remain in the image.

Symptom-specificity check: General phrases such as "something does not render correctly", "charts come out wrong" or "it should render correctly" are acceptable when the text immediately gives the context: what is affected, what kind of problem it is, or which image shows the correct result. This check fails only when such a phrase stands alone, or when a time window or region is the only explanation given.

Image-dependency check: The text should say what kind of problem it is, or point to where the correct result can be seen. The image should retain the clue that points to the cause: which instance, what triggers it, how big it is, when it happens, and the error text. If stating the expected result would give the clue away, confirm it points to a reference image ("should look like reference.png"). Example: "The shadow is missing under one of the objects on the floor, while the other object has one. Every object should cast its shadow." Verify that this names the element (the shadow), the defect (missing), and the expected result. Which object, and why, should stay in the video. The text must not describe the problem incorrectly (e.g., calling a console crash "a problem in a rendered image").
answerOptionText: [Fail - Unspecific Symptoms] The instruction does not explain beyond "something does not render correctly" / "it should work correctly" / a region or time window; or it describes the problem incorrectly; or the with-image trials show agents could not tell the bug from intended behavior.

[Non-Fail - Image-carried Symptom]: The instruction names the element and gives the context right away, but leaves the exact defect to a comparison image the text points to. Note: if in the report, it is not a fail - add this flag to feedback, if present.
The instructions.md file PASS all of the checks: instruction, symptom-specificity, & image-dependency

title: Tests - Implementation Overfit
questionText: Rate the Implementation Overfit of the Tests dimension.
questionDescription:
For each assertion ask: “would a correct fix written a different way still pass?” If a test checks exact bytes, function/file names, or a literal CSS/source string, it will cause invalid fails — loosen or drop it.

----- Context -----
When considering whether a test is overfit, we need to devise hypothetical implementations that the model could generate which the test would unfairly penalize. Additionally, we should also consider the context of the repo's pre-existing codebase—an implementation may be considered technically "valid" if it doesn't directly clash with expectations, but it's only "plausible" if it mimics pre-existing code in some way. (I.e., An experienced repo contributor would likely write the implementation in a similar way.)

Note that if an implementation does not align with well-established, intentional design choices within the repo—e.g., a reoccurring factory template or some other design pattern—then it should not be considered as "valid". (An experienced repo contributor would follow the repo's expected conventions.)

----- Important Definitions -----
A "valid" implementation solves the prompt's explicit requirements while not actively clashing with the repo's implicit expectations (e.g., established design patterns, naming conventions, etc.).

A "plausible" implementation is a valid implementation that also has any precedent in the repo. (E.g., if a pre-existing function handles something by doing XYZ, then an implementation which also does XYZ can be considered "plausible".) If there hasn't been an opportunity for the repo to establish this precedent, then general/common practice may be considered instead.

**Note**: Tests can default to applicable industry standards when prompt is imprecise or leaves room for subjectivity.

**IMPORTANT: See "Examples & Notes" tab in spec sheet for further explanation and details.**

-----
**NOTE:** do not use the sandbox to assess. Download the 4 directories, inspect, run docker, patch, and test code locally.
answerOptionText:
[Fail - Overfit Tests]
• At least one test penalizes a "plausible" implementation (see notes)
• At least one test is overfit to the golden response (exact names, bytes, layout, or an asserted source/CSS string) without cause

[Non-Fail - Slightly Overfit]
• At least one test penalizes a "valid" implementation (not "plausible")
No unit tests penalize a "valid" or "plausible" implementation.
